articles.title: I built a skyscraper you buy windows in (Node, SQLite, Stripe, Telegram Stars)
articles.excerpt: I wanted to try a weekend-sized idea: the Million Dollar Homepage, but as an endless night skyscraper. theinternettower.app – every apartment is a window. You buy one from €5, put your name, logo and…
articles.body: I wanted to try a weekend-sized idea: the Million Dollar Homepage, but as an endless night skyscraper. theinternettower.app – every apartment is a window. You buy one from €5, put your name, logo and link on it, and your rank is simply the total you've paid. The top spot is a rooftop billboard (the "penthouse"). Someone can always outbid you, but your apartment just moves down a floor – it stays yours. Just for fun. Not a startup, not an investment. How it's built Backend: zero-dependency Node (22+) with the built-in node:sqlite . No framework, no ORM. Frontend: one self-contained HTML file, no build step on the client. Payments: Stripe Checkout on the web, and Telegram Stars inside a Telegram Mini App.

articles.title: Connecting Codex CLI to the Official GitHub MCP Server on Windows Without Docker
articles.excerpt: During daily repository maintenance with Codex CLI, switching back and forth between your browser and terminal quickly becomes tedious: bug reports live in GitHub Issues, while code changes and review…
articles.body: During daily repository maintenance with Codex CLI, switching back and forth between your browser and terminal quickly becomes tedious: bug reports live in GitHub Issues, while code changes and review discussions sit inside Pull Requests (PRs). Every time you inspect a ticket, you have to open the web page, manually copy the title, body, and comments, and paste them into the terminal prompt. Whenever someone posts a new reply or the ticket status changes, you have to copy everything all over again. By connecting the official hosted GitHub MCP (Model Context Protocol) server, you allow Codex CLI to fetch the latest repository data directly from your terminal.

articles.title: The Shopify Aisle Where the Seal Renewal Quietly Stops
articles.excerpt: A Seal subscription does not usually end with a complaint. It ends in a queue nobody opened. The customer liked the product, the shipment cadence suited them, and then a card was replaced, a bank tigh…
articles.body: A Seal subscription does not usually end with a complaint. It ends in a queue nobody opened. The customer liked the product, the shipment cadence suited them, and then a card was replaced, a bank tightened a rule overnight, or a renewal landed two days before payday — and the store's ordinary order emails kept arriving while the subscription itself sat failed, unnoticed, in a different part of the dashboard. That separation is the Seal problem in miniature. In a Shopify store, a one-off order failure is visible: the customer writes in, the order is retried, someone cares that day. A subscription failure is quieter. The next shipment simply does not generate, which means there is no angry email and no abandoned-cart event to trigger anyone's attention.

articles.body: “Test macro F1 was 0.933” tells me less than “test macro F1 was 0.933, with a bootstrap standard error of 0.047 and a conditional 95% interval of 0.829–1.000.” To interpret the second result, I still need to know what was held fixed and what I varied. The overview of DIY AutoML Evaluation uses scikit-learn datasets and a TensorFlow multilayer perceptron (MLP) to explain why I save uncertainty and intermediate results. The business companion starts with an Excel workbook and the observed errors. This article explains how I calculated the intervals and drew the figures, then shows how to reproduce them. The evaluation examples use DIY AutoML 0.4.0a7. English article index Identify what can move the result Standard deviation (SD) describes the spread of a specified set of values.

Attempting to use P/Invoke ( Add-Type ) to call Win32 APIs like SetProcessDPIAware() alongside Graphics.CopyFromScreen triggers heuristic signatures for malicious screen scrapers ( ScriptContainedMaliciousContent ). articles.title: fzf Setup: What Ctrl-R, Ctrl-T and Alt-C Actually Change
articles.excerpt: The two most expensive moments in a terminal are not typing commands. They are finding the command you used last month, and finding the file buried seven directories deep whose path you only half reme…
articles.body: The two most expensive moments in a terminal are not typing commands. They are finding the command you used last month, and finding the file buried seven directories deep whose path you only half remember. fzf solves both with one fuzzy search box, but only if you install it in the right order. Most first attempts fail because three separate things get mixed together: the binary, the shell integration, and the key bindings. What fzf actually does fzf is a general-purpose fuzzy finder written in Go. Give it a list of lines on stdin, and it gives you an interactive selector: type a few non-consecutive characters, candidates are ranked by match quality, arrow keys pick one, Enter commits. That is the whole core.
articles.author: crabcheng

articles.title: A limit order book bug that only shows up after a level empties
articles.excerpt: I'd guess that most people preparing for a quant developer interview write a limit order book at some point, and I wrote a small one in Python recently to go with some practice material. I thought it…
articles.body: I'd guess that most people preparing for a quant developer interview write a limit order book at some point, and I wrote a small one in Python recently to go with some practice material. I thought it was finished, but it wasn't, and I think the way I found out is worth more than the book itself. My book keeps a dict on each side that maps a price to a queue of orders, oldest first, and it keeps a heap so that it can find the best price quickly. When a price level runs out of orders I don't bother taking it out of the heap at once. I just skip it the next time it comes to the top, which people call lazy deletion. Every test I wrote by hand passed.

articles.excerpt: From Russian masterpieces to modern dystopias, these are the books that never get old.
articles.body: Most of us treat classic literature like a checklist to conquer in high school or college and then never touch those books again. You power through the plot, underline a few quotes for a term paper, and move on to whatever else is new. The catch is that great books rarely reveal their most fascinating tricks on the first pass. When you already know the ending, your brain stops racing for answers and begins to notice the machinery holding all those mysteries and themes together. Suddenly, an unreliable narrator's sleight of hand becomes obvious, or a throwaway line in chapter two hits like a freight train in light of later developments .

articles.excerpt: Your guide to December's full Cold Moon, from peak times to skywatching highlights.
articles.body: The December full moon reaches peak illumination at 8:28 p.m. EST on Dec. 23 (0128 GMT on Dec. 24) as the lunar disk shines opposite the sun in Earth's sky. It is often called the "Cold Moon" in reference to the frigid temperatures that prevail in the Northern Hemisphere around the time of its rising, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac . December's full moon will also occur close to perigee — the moon's closest point to Earth in its elliptical orbit — giving rise to a spectacular supermoon. A supermoon can appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than a full moon at its farthest point from Earth (also known as a micromoon)..

articles.excerpt: On Nov. 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight. The M2-F3 aircraft was a heavyweight "lifting body" designed to test its ability to produce most of its lift through its fuselage instead of wings. It's commonly referred to as a "wingless" aircraft. After Air Force test pilot Bill Dana took the M2-F3 on three unpowered glide test flights, he did the first powered flight, too. Dana soared to an altitude of 45,000 feet during this flight, which lasted just over 6 minutes. He didn't break the sound barrier this time, but he did on later flights. The M2-F3 flew a total of 27 missions in its three-year flight history. Its top speed was 1.6 times the speed of sound, and its top altitude was 71,500 feet.
